children: By Martin Baccardax
Soaring government borrowing costs, large deficits, an approaching election, and political gridlock over how to repair the nation's deteriorating finances.

At first glance, you could be forgiven for thinking this is the preamble for a story on U.S. bond market risks, which have risen to multi-decade highs over the past few weeks with little response from lawmakers in Washington.

But it's also a description of what's happening in France, Europe's second-largest economy and one of the biggest bond markets in the world, with big implications for debt markets and the region's political future over the coming year.
France's borrowing premium over Germany, the eurozone's largest economy, has nearly tripled over the past eight months as investors worry about its deteriorating finances.

The extra yield, or spread, that investors demand to own 10-year government bonds issued by France, instead of triple-A-rated debt sold by Germany, has soared by nearly 100 basis points since late February to around 150 basis points this week. It reached around 160 basis points earlier this month.
Benchmark 10-year French government bond yields were recently at 4.926%, just below their early October peak of 5%, the highest in more than two decades.
For a nation with around EUR3.6 trillion in outstanding debt, rising borrowing costs pose a growing financial challenge. And it could get worse.
The government of President Emmanuel Macron is hampered by a hung National Assembly that is struggling to pass a new budget for next year.

Finance Minister Roland Lescure wants a package that includes around $48 billion in spending cuts, but that's facing stiff opposition from both the far right, including presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen, and far-left rival Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

France holds its next presidential election beginning in April, with Macron barred from seeking a third consecutive term. But the bond market's reaction to the candidates' plans, against a backdrop of the largest and most damaging protests in decades, suggests a solution may be needed well before then.

"France is now in clear crisis and decoupling from global developed bond markets," said Stephen Coltman, head of macro at 21shares, noting the recent climb in 10-year French bond yields against declines in other major markets. "And it's difficult to see how French debt returns to a stable equilibrium absent a major escalation of that crisis first."

The crisis itself is grave: the violent weekend protests have been increasing in size and scope for weeks, with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu saying police have "lost control" in several areas of the country and asking for partial curfews in response to the rioting.
France's budget deficit is likely to reach 5.4% of GDP this year, well above Europe's agreed limit of 3%, and the current proposals won't reduce it below 5% for at least two more years.
Penalties from Brussels could follow if the 3% threshold isn't met, with a larger standoff likely if Le Pen's election leads to her promised reduction in contributions to the EU budget.

It could also provide a test for the European Central Bank, whose Transmission Protection Instrument, or TPI, supports Eurozone government debt from "unwarranted" market pricing by buying French debt and injecting liquidity directly into funding markets.

"If the ECB judged the widening in spreads to reflect France-specific fiscal and political risks rather than market dysfunction, it would not want to use its TPI," said Elias Hilmer, markets economist at Capital Economics.

It may also be politically impossible to help France, with a debt-to-GDP ratio roughly twice the size of the EU's Stability and Growth pact limit, if it opts to elect a far right leader who has spoken openly about leaving both the single currency and the broader European Union.
The fact that the ECB is run by a former French finance minister, Christine Lagarde, will also weigh heavily on its ultimate decision.

That leaves the current situation, with French bond yields marching relentlessly higher, the benchmark CAC-40 stock exchange trading in negative territory for the year, and the French economy stalled in the doldrums, particularly worrying.

IMF forecasts published last week suggest France's growth this year will be less than half of the 0.9% pace recorded in 2025, and sharply trail the 1.1% pace expected for the eurozone and the 3.1% clip forecast for the global economy as a whole.

"The European establishment is trying to maneuver Le Pen into a situation in which she commits, if elected, to operating with fiscally-neutral changes to that budget," said Krisha Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI.
"But we are still a long way from that and even if it materialized, such a pledge could come unstuck next year," he added. "In the interim the bias is for spreads and yields to move higher."
That suggests comparisons to Greece's financial woes, which helped trigger Europe's sovereign debt crisis more than a decade ago, are likely to take hold.
But we're not there yet.

"Greece's credibility was destroyed by false statistics; France's is being eroded by false promises," said ING's global head of macro Carsten Brzeski, who notes that France has a fiscal problem, but not yet a funding one, given that its overall borrowing costs are still below its nominal GDP growth rate.
And Europe has programs in place today, alongside the firepower of the ECB, that didn't exist when Greece threatened the very fabric of the currency union nearly fifteen years ago.

"All of this means that fears about a new euro debt crisis are overdone," Brzeski said. "Fears about the political ability and willingness to bring national economies to reforms and sustainable public finances, unfortunately, are not."
That's a view that should be heeded in Paris, but also in Washington.
